Find them: `kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r \\'.items[] | .metadata as $m | .spec.containers[] | select(.securityContext.privileged==true) | \"\\\\($m.namespace)/\\\\($m.name)/\\\\(.name)\"\\'`\\n2. Remove `privileged: true`; grant only the specific Linux capability needed. Enforce with Pod Security Admission `restricted` or a policy engine.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  privileged: false\\n  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false\\n  capabilities:\\n    drop: [\"ALL\"]\\n    add: [\"NET_BIND_SERVICE\"]   # only if required\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/)\\n\\n### S2 \u2014 No host namespaces\\n**Why it matters:** `hostNetwork`/`hostPID`/`hostIPC` break the container isolation boundary \u2014 a pod can see host processes, sniff node traffic, or share IPC with the host.\\n**Steps:** Remove host-namespace flags from workloads (legitimate only for specific system DaemonSets). Enforce via PSA `baseline`/`restricted`.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nspec:\\n  hostNetwork: false\\n  hostPID: false\\n  hostIPC: false\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S3 / S4 / S5 \u2014 Pod hardening (allowPrivilegeEscalation / drop ALL caps / seccomp RuntimeDefault)\\n**Why it matters:** These three together close the most common privilege-escalation and syscall-abuse paths and are exactly what the PSA `restricted` profile enforces.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, drop `ALL` capabilities, and set `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` on every workload container.\\n2. Enforce cluster-wide via PSA labels on namespaces or a policy engine (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) so new workloads can\\'t regress.\\n**Snippet (container + pod securityContext):**\\n```yaml\\nspec:\\n  securityContext:\\n    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }\\n  containers:\\n    - name: ${APP}\\n      securityContext:\\n        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false\\n        runAsNonRoot: true\\n        capabilities: { drop: [\"ALL\"] }\\n```\\n**Snippet (enforce restricted on a namespace):**\\n```yaml\\nmetadata:\\n  labels:\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)\\n\\n### S6 \u2014 readOnlyRootFilesystem\\n**Why it matters:** A writable root filesystem lets an attacker drop binaries, modify config, or persist inside a running container.\\n**Steps:** Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`; mount `emptyDir` for the few paths the app must write (tmp, cache).\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true\\nvolumeMounts:\\n  - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }\\nvolumes:\\n  - { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} }\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S7 \u2014 runAsNonRoot\\n**Why it matters:** Containers running as UID 0 inherit host-root capabilities on escape. Running as a non-root user is a cheap, high-value hardening.\\n**Steps:** Set `runAsNonRoot: true` (and a concrete `runAsUser`) on workloads; rebuild images with a non-root `USER` where the process requires a fixed UID.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nsecurityContext:\\n  runAsNonRoot: true\\n  runAsUser: 1000\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S8 \u2014 No hostPath volumes\\n**Why it matters:** A `hostPath` mount exposes the node filesystem to the pod \u2014 a path to read host secrets or escape to the node.\\n**Steps:** Replace hostPath with `emptyDir`, PVCs, or CSI volumes. Where a host mount is unavoidable (system agents), restrict to a specific path and mount read-only.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n\\n### S9 \u2014 Pod Security Admission configured\\n**Why it matters:** Without PSA labels (or a policy engine), nothing stops a workload from running privileged/root/host-namespace \u2014 the hardening checks above aren\\'t enforced, only hoped for.\\n**Steps:** Label workload namespaces with PSA `enforce`/`warn`/`audit` at `baseline` or `restricted`; or run Kyverno/Gatekeeper with equivalent policies.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nmetadata:\\n  labels:\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline\\n    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)\\n\\n### S10 \u2014 No cluster-admin to non-system principals\\n**Why it matters:** A ClusterRoleBinding to `cluster-admin` for a human user, broad group, or workload SA is full cluster compromise if that identity is phished or leaked.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Find them: `kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r \\'.items[] | select(.roleRef.name==\"cluster-admin\") | \"\\\\(.metadata.name): \\\\(.subjects)\"\\'`\\n2. Replace with least-privilege roles (`view`/`edit` or custom Roles scoped to namespaces). Keep cluster-admin only for break-glass, ideally via EKS Access Entries.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Using RBAC Authorization](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/)\\n\\n### S11 \u2014 No wildcard RBAC\\n**Why it matters:** A ClusterRole with `verbs: [\"*\"]`, `resources: [\"*\"]`, or `apiGroups: [\"*\"]` is cluster-admin by another name and bypasses the intent of RBAC.\\n**Steps:** Replace wildcards with explicit verbs/resources the workload actually uses; audit with `kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq` filtering for `\"*\"` (exclude built-in `admin`/`cluster-admin`/`edit`/`system:` roles).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S12 \u2014 Access Entries / API auth mode *(AWS-API)*\\n**Why it matters:** The `aws-auth` ConfigMap is deprecated and error-prone; the Cluster Access Management API with Access Entries is the current, auditable standard.\\n**How to verify / fix:** `aws eks describe-cluster --name ${CLUSTER} --query cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode` (target `API`); migrate principals to Access Entries.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S13 \u2014 IRSA / Pod Identity for workloads\\n**Why it matters:** Workloads using the node IAM role inherit the node\\'s broad permissions. Per-workload identity (EKS Pod Identity, preferred; or IRSA) scopes AWS access to exactly what the pod needs.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Identify workloads making AWS calls via the node role (no SA annotation / Pod Identity association).\\n2. Prefer **EKS Pod Identity** (no OIDC config, supports session tags/ABAC; pre-deployed on Auto Mode); use IRSA where Pod Identity isn\\'t an option.\\n**Snippet (IRSA-annotated ServiceAccount):**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: ServiceAccount\\nmetadata:\\n  name: ${APP}-sa\\n  namespace: ${NAMESPACE}\\n  annotations:\\n    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT_ID}:role/${ROLE_NAME}\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)\\n- [EKS User Guide \u2014 EKS Pod Identities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/pod-identities.html)\\n\\n### S14 \u2014 automountServiceAccountToken disabled where unused\\n**Why it matters:** A mounted SA token a workload doesn\\'t use is a free credential for an attacker who compromises the pod \u2014 it can call the Kubernetes API as that SA.\\n**Steps:** Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the SA or pod for workloads that don\\'t call the API; leave on only where in-cluster API access is needed.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: ServiceAccount\\nmetadata: { name: ${APP}-sa, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nautomountServiceAccountToken: false\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n\\n### S15 \u2014 NetworkPolicy default-deny coverage\\n**Why it matters:** By default all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed (flat east/west). A compromised pod can reach everything. VPC CNI Network Policy is **not enabled by default** \u2014 the baseline is default-deny per namespace plus an explicit DNS allow.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Enable Network Policy on the VPC CNI addon (`ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY=true`) or use a policy-capable CNI.\\n2. Apply a default-deny (ingress+egress) per workload namespace, then a DNS-allow, then incrementally allow required flows.\\n**Snippet (default-deny + DNS allow):**\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: NetworkPolicy\\nmetadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nspec:\\n  podSelector: {}\\n  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]\\n---\\napiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: NetworkPolicy\\nmetadata: { name: allow-dns, namespace: ${NAMESPACE} }\\nspec:\\n  podSelector: {}\\n  policyTypes: [Egress]\\n  egress:\\n    - to:\\n        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }\\n          podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }\\n      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Network Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/network-security.html)\\n- [EKS User Guide \u2014 Configure your cluster for Kubernetes network policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cni-network-policy.html)\\n'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_4rG7aLzJCwMTIZNXHoLymU", "content": "[{'text': '# Security Network Nodes remediations \u2014 shard 01\\nCanonical IDs: `S16,S17,S18,S19,S20,S21,S22,S23`\\n\\n### S16 \u2014 No webhook catch-all rules\\n**Why it matters:** An admission webhook matching `apiGroups:[\"*\"]` AND `resources:[\"*\"]` intercepts every API call \u2014 a single point of failure and a latency tax on all operations.\\n**Steps:** Scope webhook `rules` to the specific apiGroups/resources/operations the webhook actually needs.\\n**References:**\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Dynamic Admission Control](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/)\\n\\n### S17 \u2014 Webhook failurePolicy on system namespaces\\n**Why it matters:** A webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` that also intercepts kube-system can block control-plane operations if the webhook backend is down \u2014 a cluster-wide outage risk.\\n**Steps:** Exempt kube-system/kube-public via `namespaceSelector`, or set `failurePolicy: Ignore` for non-critical webhooks.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\nnamespaceSelector:\\n  matchExpressions:\\n    - { key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: NotIn, values: [kube-system, kube-public] }\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Dynamic Admission Control](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/)\\n\\n### S18 \u2014 External secrets management\\n**Why it matters:** Raw Kubernetes Secrets are base64 (not encrypted) and live in etcd; sprawl of sensitive data in Secrets widens the blast radius of an etcd or RBAC compromise.\\n**Steps:** Use External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver to source secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store at runtime; pair with KMS envelope encryption (SM1).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Data encryption and secrets management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)\\n\\n### S19 \u2014 Secrets via volume not env\\n**Why it matters:** Secrets injected as env vars leak through crash dumps, `/proc`, logging, and `kubectl describe` more readily than mounted files.\\n**Steps:** Mount secrets as files (volume) instead of `env`/`envFrom`; the app reads from the mounted path.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Data encryption and secrets management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)\\n\\n### S20 \u2014 Image pull policy / no :latest\\n**Why it matters:** `:latest` (or untagged) images are non-deterministic \u2014 two pods can run different code, and rollbacks are impossible. It also defeats image provenance.\\n**Steps:** Pin explicit, immutable tags (or digests); set ECR repositories to `IMMUTABLE`; set `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` with pinned tags.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\ncontainers:\\n  - name: ${APP}\\n    image: ${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com/${REPO}:1.4.2\\n    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent\\n```\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Image Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html)\\n\\n### S21 \u2014 Image scanning present\\n**Why it matters:** Unscanned images ship known CVEs into the cluster. Continuous scanning catches them before and after deploy.\\n**Steps:** Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) on repositories, or run Trivy/Grype in CI and in-cluster.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Image Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html)\\n- [Amazon ECR \u2014 Image scanning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)\\n\\n### S22 \u2014 GuardDuty EKS protection\\n**Why it matters:** GuardDuty EKS Protection (audit-log + runtime monitoring) detects threats like crypto-mining, privilege escalation, and suspicious API calls that static checks miss.\\n**Steps:** Enable GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring and EKS Runtime Monitoring (agent auto-managed) for the account.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)\\n- [GuardDuty \u2014 EKS Protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/kubernetes-protection.html)\\n\\n### S23 \u2014 Policy enforcement engine\\n**Why it matters:** Pod Security Admission enforces only the built-in PSS levels. A policy engine (Kyverno, Gatekeeper/OPA) enforces org-specific rules at admission \u2014 required registries, no `:latest`, mandatory labels, blocked capabilities \u2014 and rejects non-compliant workloads before they run, instead of detecting them after.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Detect: `kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o name | grep -Ei \\'kyverno|gatekeeper|opa\\'` and check for the controller Deployment.\\n2. If absent and PSA alone doesn\\'t meet policy needs, deploy Kyverno or Gatekeeper and start in `audit`/`Warn` mode before enforcing.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\n# Kyverno ClusterPolicy \u2014 block :latest as an example\\napiVersion: kyverno.io/v1\\nkind: ClusterPolicy\\nmetadata: { name: disallow-latest-tag }\\nspec:\\n  validationFailureAction: Enforce\\n  rules:\\n    - name: require-image-tag\\n      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }\\n      validate:\\n        message: \"Using a mutable image tag is not allowed.\"\\n        pattern: { spec: { containers: [{ image: \"!*:latest\" }] } }\\n```\\n**N/A** if PSA `restricted` alone satisfies the requirement.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Pod Security (Policy as Code)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)\\n- [Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/) \u00b7 [Gatekeeper](https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper/website/docs/)\\n'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_6LWy05pRm5CvSgY0WHfJes", "content": "[{'text': '# Security Network Nodes remediations \u2014 shard 02\\nCanonical IDs: `S24,S25,S26,S27,S28,S29,S30,S31,SM1,SM2,SM3,SM4,SM5,SM6,SM7,S32`\\n\\n### S24 \u2014 Container-optimized node OS\\n**Why it matters:** General-purpose or custom AMIs carry a larger attack surface and a heavier patch burden than purpose-built container OSes. Bottlerocket (immutable, minimal, SELinux-enforcing) and AL2023 / EKS-optimized AMIs reduce both.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Inspect: `kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,OS:.status.nodeInfo.osImage,RUNTIME:.status.nodeInfo.containerRuntimeVersion`\\n2. Migrate general-purpose/custom AMIs to Bottlerocket or AL2023 via the MNG AMI type or Karpenter `EC2NodeClass.amiFamily`.\\n**N/A** on Fargate / Auto Mode (AWS-managed OS).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Infrastructure Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/infrastructure-security.html)\\n- [Bottlerocket](https://aws.amazon.com/bottlerocket/)\\n\\n### S25 \u2014 Minimized node access (SSM over SSH)\\n**Why it matters:** Open SSH (port 22) on worker nodes is a standing attack surface and a credential-management burden. SSM Session Manager gives audited, key-less, IAM-gated break-glass access with no inbound port.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Check for SSH exposure: launch-template key pairs and security-group rules allowing TCP 22 (especially from `0.0.0.0/0`) \u2014 AWS-API.\\n2. Remove the SSH ingress and key pairs; attach `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` to the node role and use `aws ssm start-session`.\\n**N/A** in kubectl-only mode (SG/launch-template facts need AWS-API) \u2014 flag for follow-up.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Infrastructure Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/infrastructure-security.html)\\n- [Systems Manager \u2014 Session Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html)\\n\\n### S26 \u2014 No long-lived ServiceAccount-token auth\\n**Why it matters:** A manually-created `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret is a static, non-expiring credential. If it leaks it grants the SA\\'s access until the Secret is deleted \u2014 there is no rotation. Modern clusters should use short-lived projected tokens, and AWS workloads should use IRSA / Pod Identity.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Find static SA-token Secrets: `kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token -o wide` (legacy auto-created ones are expected on older clusters; flag any used as kubeconfig credentials).\\n2. Replace with `TokenRequest`-projected volumes (auto-mounted, short-lived) for in-cluster, and IRSA / Pod Identity for AWS access; delete the static Secret after migrating.\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n- [Kubernetes \u2014 Bound Service Account Tokens](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/service-accounts/#bound-service-account-tokens)\\n\\n### S27 \u2014 EFS Access Points for shared storage\\n**Why it matters:** Mounting the EFS file-system root gives every consuming pod the same broad path and POSIX identity \u2014 one compromised or buggy app can traverse another tenant\\'s data. EFS Access Points enforce a fixed root directory and POSIX user/group per application, isolating tenants on a shared file system.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Inventory EFS-backed PVs: check the EFS CSI driver `PersistentVolume` specs for `volumeHandle` using the FS root vs an `accessPointID` (`fs-xxxx::fsap-xxxx`).\\n2. Create an Access Point per application (enforced UID/GID + root dir) and reference it in the StorageClass / PV.\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\n# EFS CSI StorageClass using an access point\\nparameters:\\n  provisioningMode: efs-ap\\n  fileSystemId: fs-0123456789abcdef0\\n  directoryPerms: \"700\"\\n```\\n**N/A** if no EFS in use or no AWS-API access.\\n**References:**\\n- [EFS \u2014 Working with access points](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/efs-access-points.html)\\n- [EFS CSI driver \u2014 Access points](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-efs-csi-driver/tree/master/examples/kubernetes/access_points)\\n\\n### S28 \u2014 IMDSv2 enforced on nodes\\n**Why it matters:** With IMDSv1, any pod that has network egress can reach `169.254.169.254` and retrieve the node\\'s **instance-profile credentials** \u2014 an SSRF/escape path to whatever the node role can do. IMDSv2 (token-required) plus a hop limit of 1 blocks pods from the metadata endpoint.\\n**Steps:**\\n1. Karpenter: set `metadataOptions` on the EC2NodeClass. MNG/self-managed: set it on the launch template (AWS-API to confirm `HttpTokens=required`, `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1`).\\n2. Also block pod access to the node IMDS at the network layer where feasible (and prefer IRSA/Pod Identity so pods never need node creds).\\n**Snippet:**\\n```yaml\\n# Karpenter EC2NodeClass\\nspec:\\n  metadataOptions:\\n    httpTokens: required          # IMDSv2 only\\n    httpPutResponseHopLimit: 1     # pods (extra hop) can\\'t reach IMDS\\n    httpEndpoint: enabled\\n```\\n**N/A** on Auto Mode (AWS-managed node config) / kubectl-only mode (launch-template is AWS-API).\\n**References:**\\n- [EKS Best Practices \u2014 Identity and Access Management (IMDS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)\\n- [EC2 \u2014 Use IMDSv2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html)\\n\\n### S29 \u2014 No anonymous / unauthenticated RBAC bindings\\n**Why it matters:** A RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding to `system:anonymous` or the `system:unauthenticated` group grants **unauthenticated** callers whatever that role allows \u2014 a direct, unauthenticated access path into the cluster. This is distinct from S10 (cluster-admin to named principals).\\n**Steps:**\\n1. **S7 — runAsNonRoot (High) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** `runAsNonRoot` is unset on the same three workloads. `hardened-app` sets it with `runAsUser: 65535`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Severity rationale and impact:** the pause image happens to run as UID 65535, but nothing enforces it. A different image would run as root and inherit host-root capabilities on escape.
- **Remediation:** set `runAsNonRoot: true` and a concrete `runAsUser` at pod level.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S5 — seccomp RuntimeDefault (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** `seccompProfile` is unset on `legacy-web`, `env-secret-app` and `hostnet-pod`. `hardened-app` uses `RuntimeDefault`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an unrestricted syscall surface for a compromised container.
- **Remediation:** `spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`.
- **Links:** [Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)

**S6 — readOnlyRootFilesystem (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** the root filesystem is writable on the same three workloads. `hardened-app` sets `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an attacker can drop binaries or modify configuration inside a running container.
- **Remediation:** set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and mount `emptyDir` for any required writable paths.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S9 — Pod Security Admission configured (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `Namespace/default` and `Namespace/team-a` have only the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label. `secure-ns` enforces `restricted`.
- **Impact:** nothing blocks privileged, host-network or root pods in the two namespaces that run user workloads. This is how `hostnet-pod` was admitted.
- **Remediation:** label with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline`, plus `warn: restricted` and `audit: restricted`.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html), [Enforce PSS with namespace labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)

**S14 — automountServiceAccountToken (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** the token is auto-mounted (projected `kube-api-access-*` volume) on `legacy-web`, `env-secret-app` and `hostnet-pod`. All three use the `default` ServiceAccount and run the pause image, so they do not call the API. `hardened-app` sets it to false. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an unused credential is available to anything that compromises the pod.
- **Remediation:** set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or pod spec.
- **Links:** [Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)

**S12 — Access Entries / API auth mode (Medium) — Persisting**

- **Impact:** the deprecated ConfigMap remains an auth path alongside access entries, and it is easy to misedit.
- **Remediation:** move the node role mapping to an access entry, validate, then move the cluster to `API` mode. The cluster already has 8 access entries.
- **Links:** [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)

- **Remediation:** adopt External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver with AWS Secrets Manager.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

- **Evidence:** `team-a/Pod/hostnet-pod` has `spec.hostNetwork: true`. Its pod IP `10.42.0.64` equals the node IP of `ip-10-42-0-64`. The pod was created 19:34:27Z.
- **Severity rationale:** a user pod shares the node's network namespace, so it can reach node-local services and bypass pod-level network controls. Nothing here enforces PSA, and there are no NetworkPolicies to compensate.
- **Impact:** a compromised pod can sniff or reach node-local traffic and any service bound to the node interface. Pods on the same node are also exposed.
- **Remediation (needs human approval):** remove `hostNetwork` and set `hostPID: false` and `hostIPC: false`. Apply PSA `baseline` or `restricted` to `team-a`.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**SM3 — Endpoint exposure (High) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `endpointPublicAccess: true`, `endpointPrivateAccess: true`, `publicAccessCidrs: ["0.0.0.0/0"]` (describe-cluster).
- **Severity rationale:** the API server is internet-reachable from any address. Authentication and authorization still apply.
- **Impact:** a larger attack surface for credential spraying and unpatched-API exploitation.
- **Remediation:** restrict `publicAccessCidrs` to known egress ranges, or disable public access since private access is already on.
- **Links:** [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)

**S32 — StorageClass encryption (High) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `StorageClass/gp2` has `provisioner: kubernetes.io/aws-ebs` and parameters `{fsType: ext4, type: gp2}`, with no `encrypted`.
- **Severity rationale:** any PVC using this class gets an unencrypted EBS volume. There are no PVCs yet, so there is no data at risk today.
- **Impact:** silent data-at-rest exposure for future volumes.
- **Remediation:** set `parameters: {type: gp3, encrypted: "true", kmsKeyId: <KMS_KEY_ARN>}` on an EBS CSI class.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

**S3 — allowPrivilegeEscalation=false (High) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** the field is unset on `default/Deployment/legacy-web`, `team-a/Deployment/env-secret-app` (both Persisting) and `team-a/Pod/hostnet-pod` (New). `hardened-app` sets it to false. `team-a/Pod/priv-pod` no longer exists (Resolved).
- **Severity rationale:** this is a one-line hardening fix, and there is no admission control to catch regressions.
- **Impact:** processes can gain privileges through setuid binaries.
- **Remediation:** set `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` on every container.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html), [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/)

**S4 — Drop ALL capabilities (High) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** no `capabilities.drop` on `legacy-web`, `env-secret-app` and `hostnet-pod`. `hardened-app` drops ALL. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Severity rationale and impact:** the default capability set is broader than needed, which widens the blast radius of a container compromise.
- **Remediation:** `capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}`, and add back only what is required.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S7 — runAsNonRoot (High) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** `runAsNonRoot` is unset on the same three workloads. `hardened-app` sets it with `runAsUser: 65535`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Severity rationale and impact:** the pause image happens to run as UID 65535, but nothing enforces it. A different image would run as root and inherit host-root capabilities on escape.
- **Remediation:** set `runAsNonRoot: true` and a concrete `runAsUser` at pod level.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S5 — seccomp RuntimeDefault (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** `seccompProfile` is unset on `legacy-web`, `env-secret-app` and `hostnet-pod`. `hardened-app` uses `RuntimeDefault`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an unrestricted syscall surface for a compromised container.
- **Remediation:** `spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`.
- **Links:** [Runtime Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/runtime-security.html)

**S6 — readOnlyRootFilesystem (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** the root filesystem is writable on the same three workloads. `hardened-app` sets `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an attacker can drop binaries or modify configuration inside a running container.
- **Remediation:** set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and mount `emptyDir` for any required writable paths.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html)

**S9 — Pod Security Admission configured (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `Namespace/default` and `Namespace/team-a` have only the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label. `secure-ns` enforces `restricted`.
- **Impact:** nothing blocks privileged, host-network or root pods in the two namespaces that run user workloads. This is how `hostnet-pod` was admitted.
- **Remediation:** label with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline`, plus `warn: restricted` and `audit: restricted`.
- **Links:** [Pod Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html), [Enforce PSS with namespace labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/enforce-standards-namespace-labels/)

**S14 — automountServiceAccountToken (Medium) — Persisting, New, Resolved**
- **Evidence:** the token is auto-mounted (projected `kube-api-access-*` volume) on `legacy-web`, `env-secret-app` and `hostnet-pod`. All three use the `default` ServiceAccount and run the pause image, so they do not call the API. `hardened-app` sets it to false. `priv-pod` is removed.
- **Impact:** an unused credential is available to anything that compromises the pod.
- **Remediation:** set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or pod spec.
- **Links:** [Identity and Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html)

**S12 — Access Entries / API auth mode (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `authenticationMode: API_AND_CONFIG_MAP`. `kube-system/ConfigMap/aws-auth` still maps the node role (`mapRoles`).
- **Impact:** the deprecated ConfigMap remains an auth path alongside access entries, and it is easy to misedit.
- **Remediation:** move the node role mapping to an access entry, validate, then move the cluster to `API` mode. The cluster already has 8 access entries.
- **Links:** [Cluster Access Management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/cluster-access-management.html)

**S18 — External secrets management (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** no ExternalSecret, SealedSecret or SecretProviderClass resource types exist. The Secrets Store CSI driver DaemonSet is not installed. `env-secret-app` reads `app-creds` as a native Secret.
- **Impact:** secret material lives only in etcd, which has no KMS envelope encryption (SM1).
- **Remediation:** adopt External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver with AWS Secrets Manager.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

**S19 — Secrets via volume, not env (Low) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `team-a/Deployment/env-secret-app` sets `DB_PASSWORD` from `secretKeyRef` (`app-creds`/`password`). The value was not read.
- **Remediation:** mount the secret as a file volume.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

**S21 — Image scanning present (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** no in-cluster scanner was detected. Inspector status is unreadable (AccessDenied), so registry-side scanning is unverified.
- **Remediation:** enable ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) or run Trivy or Grype in CI and in the cluster.
- **Links:** [Image Security](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html), [ECR image scanning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)

**S23 — Policy enforcement engine (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** the Kyverno `clusterpolicies` and Gatekeeper `constraints` resource types are not served. PSA `restricted` covers only `secure-ns`, so the N/A exception does not apply.
- **Impact:** no admission-time enforcement for `default` or `team-a`.
- **Remediation:** deploy Kyverno or Gatekeeper in audit or warn mode, then enforce.
- **Links:** [Pod Security (policy as code)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/pod-security.html), [Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/), [Gatekeeper](https://open-policy-agent.github.io/gatekeeper/website/docs/)

**S30 — VPC flow logs (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `describe-flow-logs` for `vpc-00000000000000001` and both cluster subnets returned `[]`.
- **Impact:** no network forensic record for intrusion or exfiltration investigations.
- **Remediation:** enable VPC-level flow logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
- **Links:** [VPC flow logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html)

**S36 — VPC CNI dedicated IAM role (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** the `vpc-cni` add-on has no `serviceAccountRoleArn` and no Pod Identity association (0 in the cluster). The node role carries `AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy`.
- **Impact:** any pod that can reach IMDS inherits CNI network permissions. IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 (S28 PASS) mitigates this.
- **Remediation:** create a dedicated Pod Identity or IRSA role for `aws-node`, then detach the CNI policy from the node role.
- **Links:** [VPC CNI best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/vpc-cni.html)

**SM1 — KMS envelope encryption (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `describe-cluster` has no `encryptionConfig`.
- **Remediation:** associate a customer-managed KMS key for `secrets`.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)

**SM2 — Audit logging enabled (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** logging is `api: enabled`. `audit`, `authenticator`, `controllerManager` and `scheduler` are disabled.
- **Impact:** no API audit trail for forensics, and Control Plane Health queries cannot run.
- **Remediation:** enable at least `audit` and `authenticator`.
- **Links:** [Auditing and Logging](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/auditing-and-logging.html)

**SM4 — EBS/EFS encryption at rest (Medium) — Persisting**
- **Evidence:** `StorageClass/gp2` has no `encrypted`. The node root volumes `vol-00000000000000002` and `vol-00000000000000001` report `Encrypted: false`.
- **Remediation:** encrypt the StorageClass (see S32). For nodes, set `Encrypted: true` in the launch template and roll the nodegroup, or enable EBS encryption by default for the account and region.
- **Links:** [Data encryption & secrets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/data-encryption-and-secrets-management.html)
